# Chapter 3 Practice: Stoichiometry

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/stoichiometry.md`), grouped by objective. 26 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats. Within each objective the questions run from easier to harder.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1a}} · *multiple-choice* One mole of any substance contains

A. 12.00 g of that substance
B. $6.022\times10^{23}$ elementary entities
C. 1.008 g of hydrogen
D. the same mass as one mole of carbon
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** A mole is a fixed *count*, $6.022\times10^{23}$ entities, not a fixed mass. The mass of one mole depends on the substance.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1a}} · *short answer* The periodic table lists chlorine's atomic mass as 35.45 amu, but no chlorine atom weighs 35.45 amu. Explain.
:::
::: tab Answer
35.45 amu is an **average atomic mass** — the abundance-weighted average over chlorine's naturally occurring isotopes, mainly $\ce{^{35}Cl}$ and $\ce{^{37}Cl}$. Individual atoms have masses near 35 or 37; the tabulated value describes the natural mixture, not any single atom.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1a}} · *workout* Boron has two stable isotopes: $\ce{^{10}B}$ (10.013 amu, 19.9%) and $\ce{^{11}B}$ (11.009 amu, 80.1%). Calculate boron's average atomic mass.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$10.013\times0.199 + 11.009\times0.801 = 1.993 + 8.818 = 10.81\ \text{amu}$$

Check for sense: the answer lies between the two isotope masses and much closer to 11.009, which is right because $\ce{^{11}B}$ is four times as abundant.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1a}} · *workout* Silver has two stable isotopes, $\ce{^{107}Ag}$ (106.905 amu) and $\ce{^{109}Ag}$ (108.905 amu), and an average atomic mass of 107.87 amu. Find the percent abundance of each.
:::
::: tab Answer
Let $x$ be the fraction that is $\ce{^{107}Ag}$; then $1-x$ is $\ce{^{109}Ag}$.

$$106.905x + 108.905(1-x) = 107.87$$
$$-2.000x = -1.035 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 0.518$$

So **51.8% $\ce{^{107}Ag}$** and **48.2% $\ce{^{109}Ag}$**.

This is Q3 run backwards: there you were given abundances and found the average; here you are given the average and find the abundances.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1b}} · *workout* How many moles are in 25.0 g of $\ce{CO2}$ (44.01 g/mol)?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$25.0\,\text{g}\,\ce{CO2}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}}{44.01\ \text{g}}=0.568\ \text{mol}\ \ce{CO2}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1b}} · *workout* What is the mass of 3.75 mol of $\ce{NaCl}$ (58.44 g/mol)?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$3.75\,\text{mol}\times\frac{58.44\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}}=219\ \text{g}\ \ce{NaCl}$$

Note that this conversion factor is the inverse of the one in Q5. Write it so that "mol" cancels.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1b}} · *workout* How many oxygen **atoms** are present in 12.0 g of $\ce{O2}$?
:::
::: tab Answer
Three steps, and the last is the one people miss.

$$12.0\,\text{g}\,\ce{O2}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}\ \ce{O2}}{32.00\ \text{g}}=0.375\ \text{mol}\ \ce{O2}$$
$$0.375\,\text{mol}\times\frac{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{molecules}}{1\ \text{mol}}=2.26\times10^{23}\ \text{molecules}\ \ce{O2}$$
$$2.26\times10^{23}\ \text{molecules}\times\frac{2\ \text{atoms}\ \ce{O}}{1\ \text{molecule}}=4.52\times10^{23}\ \text{atoms}\ \ce{O}$$

The question asks for **atoms**, not molecules, and each $\ce{O2}$ molecule contains two of them.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1c}} · *workout* Calculate the molar mass of $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
The subscript 2 applies to the whole hydroxide group, so this formula holds one Mg, two O, and two H.

$$24.31 + 2(16.00) + 2(1.008) = 24.31 + 32.00 + 2.016 = 58.33\ \text{g/mol}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1c}} · *short answer* Explain why chemists speak of the *formula mass* of $\ce{CaCl2}$ but the *molecular mass* of $\ce{CCl4}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
$\ce{CCl4}$ is a molecular compound made of discrete $\ce{CCl4}$ molecules, so "molecular mass" describes a real particle.

$\ce{CaCl2}$ is ionic — a lattice of $\ce{Ca^2+}$ and $\ce{Cl^-}$ ions in a 1:2 ratio, with no discrete "$\ce{CaCl2}$ molecule" anywhere in it. The formula gives a ratio, so the corresponding mass is called a formula mass. The arithmetic is identical either way.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1c}} · *workout* Calculate the percent composition of ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Molar mass: $14.01 + 3(1.008) = 17.03$ g/mol.

$$\%\,\ce{N}=\frac{14.01}{17.03}\times100\%=82.25\%$$
$$\%\,\ce{H}=\frac{3.024}{17.03}\times100\%=17.75\%$$

Check: $82.25 + 17.75 = 100.00\%$. ✓

Note that ammonia is three-quarters hydrogen by atom count but under 18% hydrogen by mass.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1c}} · *workout* Iron is extracted from two common ores: hematite, $\ce{Fe2O3}$ (159.7 g/mol), and magnetite, $\ce{Fe3O4}$ (231.5 g/mol). Which contains more iron per gram of ore?
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\%\,\ce{Fe}\ \text{in}\ \ce{Fe2O3}=\frac{2(55.85)}{159.7}\times100\%=69.94\%$$
$$\%\,\ce{Fe}\ \text{in}\ \ce{Fe3O4}=\frac{3(55.85)}{231.5}\times100\%=72.38\%$$

**Magnetite** is the richer ore, 72.38% iron against 69.94%.

Comparing formulas alone would not answer this — $\ce{Fe3O4}$ has more iron atoms but also a larger molar mass. Percent composition is what makes the two comparable per gram.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1d}} · *workout* Combustion of 1.000 g of a hydrocarbon gives 3.14 g $\ce{CO2}$ and 1.29 g $\ce{H2O}$. Determine its empirical formula.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\ce{C}:\ 3.14\,\text{g}\,\ce{CO2}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}\,\ce{CO2}}{44.01\ \text{g}}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}\,\ce{C}}{1\ \text{mol}\,\ce{CO2}}=0.0713\ \text{mol}$$
$$\ce{H}:\ 1.29\,\text{g}\,\ce{H2O}\times\frac{1\ \text{mol}\,\ce{H2O}}{18.02\ \text{g}}\times\frac{2\ \text{mol}\,\ce{H}}{1\ \text{mol}\,\ce{H2O}}=0.1432\ \text{mol}$$

Divide both by the smaller (0.0713): C 1.00, H 2.01 → ratio 1 : 2.

The empirical formula is $\ce{CH2}$.

No oxygen-by-difference step is needed here, because the problem states the compound is a hydrocarbon — only C and H are present.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 3.1d}} · *workout* A compound contains 40.00% C, 6.71% H, and 53.29% O by mass, and its molar mass is 180.16 g/mol. Find its empirical and molecular formulas.
:::
::: tab Answer
Assume a 100 g sample, so the percentages become grams.

$$\ce{C}:\ \frac{40.00}{12.01}=3.331\ \text{mol}\qquad \ce{H}:\ \frac{6.71}{1.008}=6.657\ \text{mol}\qquad \ce{O}:\ \frac{53.29}{16.00}=3.331\ \text{mol}$$

Divide by the smallest (3.331): C 1.00, H 2.00, O 1.00. Empirical formula **$\ce{CH2O}$**.

Empirical formula mass: $12.01+2(1.008)+16.00=30.03$ g/mol.

$$\frac{180.16}{30.03}=6.00$$

Multiply each subscript by 6: the molecular formula is **$\ce{C6H12O6}$** — glucose.

The molar mass is essential here. Combustion or percent data alone give only the ratio; the molar mass tells you how many times that ratio repeats.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2a}} · *multiple-choice* Which of the following may be changed when balancing a chemical equation?

A. The subscripts in a formula
B. The coefficients in front of formulas
C. The identity of the products
D. Both A and B
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** Only coefficients may change. Altering a subscript changes the substance itself — $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{H2O2}$ are different compounds, not different amounts of the same one.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2a}} · *workout* Balance $\ce{Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Iron first: $\ce{Fe2O3}$ has 2 Fe, so put a 2 on Fe. Oxygen: the right side has 3 O, but $\ce{O2}$ supplies pairs, giving a coefficient of 3/2.

$$\ce{2Fe + 3/2 O2 -> Fe2O3}$$

Clear the fraction by doubling everything:

$$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$

Check: Fe 4 = 4, O 6 = 6. ✓
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2a}} · *workout* Balance $\ce{C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O}$ (propane combustion).
:::
::: tab Answer
Balance carbon and hydrogen first, leaving oxygen for last because it appears in both products.

C: 3 on the left, so a 3 on $\ce{CO2}$. H: 8 on the left, so a 4 on $\ce{H2O}$.

$$\ce{C3H8 + O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$

O on the right: $3(2)+4(1)=10$ atoms, so $\ce{O2}$ needs a coefficient of 5.

$$\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$$

Check: C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 10. ✓

Here the oxygen came out even and no doubling was needed — unlike the ethane case in the study guide. Balance C and H first and let oxygen tell you whether scaling is required.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2b}} · *workout* For $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$, how many moles of water form from 5.0 mol of $\ce{H2}$ (with oxygen in excess)?
:::
::: tab Answer
The mole ratio comes straight from the coefficients, 2 mol $\ce{H2}$ to 2 mol $\ce{H2O}$, or 1:1.

$$5.0\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2}\times\frac{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2O}}{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2}}=5.0\ \text{mol}\ \ce{H2O}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2b}} · *workout* For $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$, what mass of $\ce{NH3}$ can be produced from 28.0 g of $\ce{N2}$, with hydrogen in excess?
:::
::: tab Answer
Walk the road map: mass → moles → mole ratio → mass.

$$28.0\,\text{g}\,\ce{N2}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{N2}}{28.02\,\text{g}}\times\frac{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{NH3}}{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{N2}}\times\frac{17.03\,\text{g}\,\ce{NH3}}{1\,\text{mol}}=34.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{NH3}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2b}} · *workout* For $\ce{2Al + 3Cl2 -> 2AlCl3}$, what mass of $\ce{Cl2}$ is required to react completely with 10.0 g of Al?
:::
::: tab Answer
The target is now a *reactant* rather than a product, but the road is unchanged — only the mole ratio differs.

$$10.0\,\text{g}\,\ce{Al}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Al}}{26.98\,\text{g}}\times\frac{3\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Cl2}}{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Al}}\times\frac{70.90\,\text{g}\,\ce{Cl2}}{1\,\text{mol}}=39.4\ \text{g}\ \ce{Cl2}$$

Reading the ratio off the correct pair of coefficients (3 and 2, not 3 and 1) is the whole difficulty here.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2c}} · *short answer* Two students disagree. One says the limiting reagent is whichever reactant you have the fewest moles of. Explain why that is wrong.
:::
::: tab Answer
The limiting reagent is the one that runs out first *given the ratio the equation requires*, not the one present in the smallest amount.

In $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$ with 2.00 mol $\ce{N2}$ and 3.00 mol $\ce{H2}$, hydrogen is more abundant yet still limiting, because the reaction demands three times as much of it. Dividing each amount by its own coefficient ($2.00/1 = 2.00$ against $3.00/3 = 1.00$) is what makes the comparison fair.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2c}} · *workout* For $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$, you have 4.0 mol $\ce{H2}$ and 3.0 mol $\ce{O2}$. Identify the limiting reagent and the moles of water formed.
:::
::: tab Answer
Divide each by its coefficient: $\ce{H2}$ gives $4.0/2 = 2.0$; $\ce{O2}$ gives $3.0/1 = 3.0$.

The smaller quotient identifies **$\ce{H2}$ as limiting**.

$$4.0\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2}\times\frac{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2O}}{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{H2}}=4.0\ \text{mol}\ \ce{H2O}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2c}} · *workout* For $\ce{Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2}$, 15.0 g of Zn is added to 15.0 g of HCl. Which is limiting, and how many grams of the excess reagent remain?
:::
::: tab Answer
**Moles of each:**
$$\ce{Zn}:\ \frac{15.0}{65.38}=0.2294\ \text{mol}\qquad \ce{HCl}:\ \frac{15.0}{36.46}=0.4114\ \text{mol}$$

**Divide by coefficients:** Zn gives $0.2294/1 = 0.2294$; HCl gives $0.4114/2 = 0.2057$.

The smaller quotient belongs to HCl, so **HCl is limiting**.

**Excess remaining.** Zn actually consumed:
$$0.4114\,\text{mol}\,\ce{HCl}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Zn}}{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{HCl}}=0.2057\ \text{mol}\ \ce{Zn}$$
$$\ce{Zn}\ \text{left}=0.2294-0.2057=0.0237\ \text{mol}\ \Rightarrow\ 0.0237\times65.38=1.55\ \text{g}\ \ce{Zn}$$

Equal masses do not mean equal moles — the two reactants have very different molar masses, which is exactly why the mole conversion has to come first.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2d}} · *short answer* A student reports a percent yield of 108%. What does this most likely indicate?
:::
::: tab Answer
Not a better-than-perfect reaction — that is impossible, since the theoretical yield is the ceiling set by the limiting reagent.

It almost always means the product was weighed while still containing something else: residual solvent, water, or unreacted starting material. Drying the product to constant mass usually brings the yield below 100%. A calculation error in the theoretical yield is the other possibility worth checking.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2d}} · *workout* A reaction has a theoretical yield of 45.0 g and an actual yield of 38.2 g. Calculate the percent yield.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\%\ \text{Yield}=\frac{38.2}{45.0}\times100\%=84.9\%$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 25
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2d}} · *workout* For $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$, heating 25.0 g of $\ce{CaCO3}$ (100.09 g/mol) yields 12.5 g of CaO (56.08 g/mol). Calculate the theoretical yield and the percent yield.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Theoretical yield**, from the 1:1 mole ratio:
$$25.0\,\text{g}\,\ce{CaCO3}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}}{100.09\,\text{g}}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{CaO}}{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{CaCO3}}\times\frac{56.08\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mol}}=14.0\ \text{g}\ \ce{CaO}$$

**Percent yield:**
$$\frac{12.5}{14.0}\times100\%=89.2\%$$

The theoretical yield is always calculated, never measured. Only the actual yield comes off a balance.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 26
{{sp[info] Objective 3.2d}} · *workout* For $\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$, 10.0 g of Na reacts with 10.0 g of $\ce{Cl2}$ and 14.9 g of NaCl is recovered. Find the limiting reagent, the theoretical yield, and the percent yield.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Moles:** $\ce{Na}$: $10.0/22.99 = 0.435$ mol. $\ce{Cl2}$: $10.0/70.90 = 0.1410$ mol.

**Divide by coefficients:** Na gives $0.435/2 = 0.2175$; $\ce{Cl2}$ gives $0.1410/1 = 0.1410$. **$\ce{Cl2}$ is limiting.**

**Theoretical yield**, from the limiting reagent only:
$$0.1410\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Cl2}\times\frac{2\,\text{mol}\,\ce{NaCl}}{1\,\text{mol}\,\ce{Cl2}}\times\frac{58.44\,\text{g}}{1\,\text{mol}}=16.5\ \text{g}\ \ce{NaCl}$$

**Percent yield:**
$$\frac{14.9}{16.5}\times100\%=90.4\%$$

This question chains all three skills — limiting reagent, then theoretical yield, then percent yield — which is how they normally appear on an exam.
:::
::::
